narrativeProgression.description: Monica shares her background, living in Spain since 1981 and getting her PhD.
Reflects on Spain's transition from dictatorship to democracy.
Discusses the challenges of living in Spain as a female migrant.

Highlights negative changes, including increased racism.
Acknowledges positive changes, particularly among young people and women.
Expresses sadness about South Sudan's separation and ongoing wars.
Shares her current involvement in teaching and research at Ahfad University for Women.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I have been living in Spain since 1980. That's like 29 years. And in 2008 I had my PhD from
the University of Granada. Before I answer this I would just like to say that when I went to
Spain at that time, Spain was just the moment of the transition from the dictatorship of Franco at that time to the democracy.

So Spain was a specific place at that time. Actually I liked it because coming out from this 40 years of regime, coming to the democracy and the new freedom and society was opening for every, in all respects, it reminds me a lot of Sudan right now because we are going through the same regime.

Living in Spain as a female migrant was not easy at all. But I have to tell that at that time in the beginning of the 1980, there were not many African female migrants. So I was like a kind of something different.

And because I went to Spain to study, I didn't went as the migration in Spain right now, it's for economic reasons, those people who are escaping from war, poverty, etc. This was not my case actually. Actually yes, I did go out from Sudan because at that time with a regime of Mimeri, they started with the Sharia things and that was the moment to leave the country I think. Although Sudan at that time was much better than now.

Living there almost 30 years, of course, Spain became my second or maybe first place, first country. Because then I lived more years in Spain than in Sudan. I spent the best of my life, my use, my time of knowledge.

I did everything in this moment in Spain. Then for me at that time coming back to Sudan, even when I used to come on vacation, I just found myself totally lost in Sudan. And believe me, it's not easy to belong to culture and sometimes not to belong to none of them. It's difficult, you know.

Now the other part of the question coming back to Sudan, coming back to Sudan for me was a big challenge and I really chose, I had this choice, I wanted to come back to Sudan and after finishing my PhD, I wanted to work in the teaching and for me, Ahmadiyy University for Women was the best place and I'm so happy that I belong into this place now.

But I discovered that Sudan is not a fat, you know, there are so many things going on in a fat, but Sudan is a huge country and actually I don't have that much time, I'm not doing so much social life or whatever. But I know that there are a lot of things going on.

But it was for me many things that I saw in Sudan after coming back last year, I came back last year in 2010, everything is shocking. I think there is more racism now in Sudan because of the political situation, because of what happened in South Sudan and what's going on in there for.

I think the people, not the government, the people of the regular people, they're changing their mind are changing, I think the attitude, I can't really swear that there is more racism now, I could tell, this is by the one hand.
In the other hand, the situation of women has deteriorated a lot. Women now are in worse, much worse situation than they used to be in our time, in the 70 and 80.
I think the women have gone backwards, not the women, but their situation, their legal situation, the social situation. And these two aspects are so important for me.

Plus the economical situation and how people are living and the economic crisis and many things has changed. But there are positive thoughts, I mean I can't see the young people moving, can see many women trying to do things and doing really great jobs.

And then we have the bad news of the sessions, the separation of the South Sudan, which is a bad news. But it is good news for those who choose them and I'm really glad for them and I really wish them the best of luck that they can have their new nation, new state and do it better than us, we from the South of Sudan.
I am involved in the master of the gender and peace and I'm teaching the gender and media, the production, peace and conflicts.
These issues are basics and next semester I'm going to be teaching the gender and human rights in Africa and Middle East.

I think in this way I could say that I'm kind of contributing to improve the situation of women by the knowledge, by have these students and even for me it's a reflective process to see how the situation of women from different aspects, how the situation of women in the conflict, time in the peace time especially Sudan has gone through the worst and the worst.
The worst and the longest war in the South and we still have war in the West and Sudan is a workplace actually it seems to.
So to see the situation of women and how the women could be involved in the peace process, in the democracy building, in the new Sudan, which is very difficult and very hard.
I mean these goals are difficult right now but at least being there in this academic course it's enabled me to get to know good students, good women who really want to do things.

And at the same time I could see there are so many women organizations in Sudan which are doing great jobs and doing good things but they still need support, space where they can achieve their goals, freedom of movement and of expressing their works and the media has a lot of problems especially for the women issues.
So I think there are so many obstacles but women are there and doing their best and this is good sign.
